title: AMD Says Its MEXT Software Keeps 95% of Server Performance on Half the DRAM
dek: AMD says MEXT memory-tiering software let an internal Synopsys workload keep 95% of performance with half its DRAM. The figures are AMD's own, and the benchmark footnotes are unpublished.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: Two 8 GB DDR4 memory modules from Corsair on a black background

keyPoints: AMD says servers running Synopsys PrimeTime kept 95% of full performance with half their DRAM, and 80% with a quarter, according to figures shared with Tom's Hardware.
MEXT moves cold memory pages to NVMe flash and uses a predictive model to bring pages back before they are requested. AMD acquired the company in June.
MEXT runs on 145 AMD servers today and is slated for 2,000 next year. HPE 'MEXT Ready' EPYC Venice servers are in phase one; license sales have no start date.
AMD published no benchmark footnotes, so the figures are first-party and unverified. Meridian treats the DRAM-cut claim as a watch item for memory makers.
body:
## What AMD claims

AMD says servers running Synopsys PrimeTime, a chip-timing tool, kept 95% of full-memory performance with half their DRAM, and 80% with a quarter of it. The figures were shared with Tom's Hardware ([Tom's Hardware](https://tomshardware.com/pc-components/cpus/amd-shares-how-it-can-retain-95-percent-of-server-performance-with-just-half-the-dram-sidestepping-memory-shortages-with-mext-tech-powers-over-100-servers-already-running-with-plans-to-expand-to-2-000-servers-in-2027)). ChipDispatch notes that AMD reported the numbers itself and has not published the benchmark footnotes ([ChipDispatch](https://chipdispatch.com/articles/amd-claims-mext-software-halves-server-dram-at-95-performance)).

## How MEXT works

MEXT is a memory-tiering product AMD bought in June, without disclosing terms. It moves cold memory pages to a dedicated NVMe drive and uses a predictive model to bring pages back into DRAM before applications request them, so the operating system still sees the full capacity. Tom's Hardware reports that the model runs on a single EPYC core without a GPU and keeps learning during the workload.

Founder Gary Smerdon, now an AMD corporate vice president, cited Meta research showing that 50% to 80% of memory pages had not been accessed for at least five minutes ([Notebookcheck](https://www.notebookcheck.net/AMD-s-new-trick-lets-servers-use-half-as-much-DRAM-with-minimal-performance-loss.1448188.0.html)). AMD says the approach can cut physical DRAM by 20% to 75%, depending on the application and performance target ([MLQ.ai](https://mlq.ai/news/amd-says-mext-software-lets-its-servers-run-on-half-the-dram-with-95-of-the-performance)). Those are AMD's ranges, not independent results.

## Deployment is still small

AMD runs MEXT on 145 internal servers and plans to extend it to 2,000 servers next year. HPE is shipping EPYC Venice servers with a "MEXT Ready" badge and a dedicated NVMe drive or bay. The second phase, which bundles MEXT licenses, has no start date ([ChipDispatch](https://chipdispatch.com/articles/amd-claims-mext-software-halves-server-dram-at-95-performance)). For now this is a roadmap, not broad availability.

## Why memory makers should care

The pitch lands in a DRAM shortage that MLQ.ai attributes to AI servers ([MLQ.ai](https://mlq.ai/news/amd-says-mext-software-lets-its-servers-run-on-half-the-dram-with-95-of-the-performance)). Smerdon told Notebookcheck that memory can account for 60% to 90% of the cost of large servers, which is why a cut in DRAM per server would matter to buyers. If tiering of this kind spreads, DRAM-per-server demand could soften. The claim is too early and too AMD-sourced to call a trend.

## What to watch

The unpublished footnotes, independent benchmarks, and whether the Phase 2 licenses ship. The 2,000-server internal rollout planned for next year is the next checkable milestone.

marketImpact.summary: AMD gains a software differentiator for EPYC servers if the claims hold, but no pricing, licensing revenue or customer volume has been disclosed. If memory tiering spreads, DRAM-per-server demand could soften, a risk for memory makers. The figures are AMD's own, and deployment is 145 internal servers, so confidence is low.
